articles.title: Are They Out There? 7 Things You Should Do If You Think You Saw a UFO
articles.content:
I want to believe.
Yes, that’s the tagline for The X-Files, the ’90s television phenomenon that I have watched in its entirety more times than I care to admit. But it’s also a credo of sorts, not just for Fox Mulder, but for tons of people all over the world who have had a close encounter with an unidentified flying object (UFO), now known by the way-less-catchy “unidentified anomalous phenomena,” or UAP.
Have you seen one? I’m still waiting—as far as I know—but I’m not nearly as cranky about the idea as Agent Scully. Our current government is all over it: Since January 2026, they’ve released hundreds of files collected since 1950 under a new program called PURSUE, or the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters. The fifth bulk file release just dropped on Aug. 7.
Coming up, I’ll take you through what to do if (uh, when!) you see a UFO or UAP and tell you how you can report your sighting to authorities, the internet, Hollywood and anyone else who might find your story fascinating and totally worth investigating. Read on to learn the seven things you should do if you spot a UFO.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more curiosities, news, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
It depends on who’s tracking the reports.
The official government repository is called the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), and their latest publicly available report, covering fiscal year 2025, lists 319 sightings—114 of which were “resolved,” meaning they turned out to be “prosaic objects such as balloons, satellites, birds, aircraft and unmanned aerial systems (UAS).”
If 319 sightings seems kind of low for a whole year, it’s good to stop here and mention that the AARO only takes reports from current or former government officials, service members and contractors. So my mother-in-law, who swears up and down that she’s seen a UAP—and can recount it in minute detail—is not counted among the number.
For regular people like her (and maybe you), the go-to repositories are the National UFO Reporting Center, aka NUFORC, which has been around since 1974, and the Mutual UFO Network, or MUFON, which has been investigating UFOs since 1969. Both have very detailed online databases that break down sightings by report date and location, as well as juicier categories like how dramatic the sightings are.
So far this year, NUFORC has received more than 1,800 reports of UAPs. In recent years, they’ve cited numbers ranging from a low of just under 4,000 reports (in 2018) to nearly 8,000 (in 2020). MUFON says they get between 500 and 1,000 reports per month.
In addition to NUFORC and MUFON, there are plenty of resources that collect and compile UAP sightings these days, but before you race to one of them with a video of your neighbor’s annoying but benign new drone, it’s worth figuring out what you might be seeing so you can report it to the right people—if at all.
Here’s what to do.
The vast majority of UAPs are not proof of alien visitors, or even particularly compelling evidence of them. Are you near an airport? Is it meteor season? Did Walmart start doing drone deliveries and ever since that godforsaken day you’ve heard nothing but the nonstop flight pattern over your house? (That’s probably just me.)
If none of those apply, grab your phone.
Take photos or a video of the object. According to NASA, you should also note the following:
This might seem old school, but NASA’s Night Sky Network is a searchable database of astronomy clubs across the U.S., and the space agency says your next step should be to contact one of them. Astronomy clubs are filled with knowledgeable people who make it a habit of watching the skies, and one of them will be more than happy to discuss your sighting and offer plausible explanations based on their expertise.
Figure out what the night sky should look like right above you using Stellarium, an app and website that reconstructs the sky based on your location and the time and date. See what stars and planets are visible, where the moon will be (or was) and the locations of other celestial bodies.
See what’s flying above you right now using free online tools and apps like FlightAware and Flightradar24, which offer live tracking of planes in the air all over the world. Satellite Tracker by Star Walk is a popular app that allows you to track Starlink and other satellites, the Hubble telescope, the International Space Station and tons of other space traffic.
Starlink satellites in particular leave a telltale (and very UFO-like) line of lights, often called a “satellite train,” when they are being positioned. Findstarlink.com tracks these trains and can be used to compare your sighting to known satellites.
This is for more technologically advanced UFO sleuths. Siterec, which is short for “situational recreation,” is an app developed to analyze UAP videos taken by sailors in the U.S. Navy, but it’s now available for anyone to use.
Drop your UFO video into the app, and it recreates what was going on at the same place and time, including in the sky and any terrain in the shot (this recreation is called a “sitch”). Then, line up and compare the sitch with your UAP video to see if your sighting can be explained by known objects or phenomena.
If after all that work you still think your UAP could be a real UFO, it’s time to report it. If you happen to be a member of the military or a government worker or contractor, AARO’s handy online reporting tool is for you. For the rest of us, NUFORC and MUFON are the gold standards.
But newer players in UAP reporting are available too. Enigma is probably the most popular. It’s an online and app-based reporting tool that lets you upload photos and videos, record details of your sighting, search a map and database and get notifications about reported sightings.
Most of the time, reporting the UAP will be its own reward. Congrats! You have just helped advance science and curiosity by uploading data that may help current and future citizens of planet Earth discover … well, we’re not quite sure what, just yet.
If you’re looking for someone to come investigate what you saw, give your report to MUFON. Each sighting is assigned a field investigator who will reach out to you to get more details about your UAP sighting.
If your video is compelling, you can always contact the media or post the vid on your socials. Who knows, maybe other people saw the same thing! Use this opportunity to meet and talk to other UAP enthusiasts, or join a local astronomy club to learn more about the cosmos. If it turns out that we are not alone, safety in numbers can’t hurt.

articles.title: This Is Prince William and Kate Middleton’s Biggest Fear for Prince George
articles.content:
There’s a lot to be concerned about when you’re a parent—not least keeping your kids fed, safe and happy—and that’s before the additional worries that come with raising a future king. Every parent wants to believe they’ve done a good job and shaped their children to be polite, confident and well-balanced, but most of our little princes and princesses don’t regularly meet world leaders!
Safety is always front of mind—balancing the need to give your kids freedom as they hit their teens and making sure they’re shielded from harm, in real life and online. And that’s something William and Kate have taken very seriously, wanting George, Charlotte and Louis to have as “normal” an upbringing as possible, while understanding their situation is anything but normal.
However, there’s one issue above all others that’s worrying William and Kate, and parents everywhere will surely relate. Read on to learn their biggest concern as 13-year-old Prince George heads to Eton this fall.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more royals, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
It’s smartphones. William and Kate have been vocal about not letting their children have mobile phones, but once George follows in his father’s footsteps to the prestigious Eton boarding school in Berkshire, west of London, they may have to grapple with some modern realities.
“There are parental concerns, naturally, that he will be growing up in a digital age,” says royal editor Rebecca English in the Daily Mail. “The couple have refused to allow their children to have mobile phones, although admit that will change with their eldest at senior school.”
No, not yet.
“Our children don’t have phones,” William told Brazilian TV host Luciano Huck last November. “I think when George moves on to secondary school, then maybe he might have a phone that has limited access,” adding that it’s a “tense” issue but that they’ve communicated to George why the internet in particular poses a problem.
Eton, which costs about $88,000 a year, has a no-smartphones policy for incoming Year 9 pupils like George, issuing them Nokia “brick phones” instead, which can’t access the internet. That’s probably reassuring for William and Kate.
“I think children can access too much stuff they don’t need to see online,” William told Huck. “And so having a phone and text message, the old sort of ‘brick phone’ as they call them, I think that’s fine.”
There are two issues. One is that this is the first time George will be fully boarding away from home—and away from his parents’ watchful eyes. Even if he does only have a brick phone, he’ll have the freedom to text his friends as much as he wants.
The second issue is that his parents can’t control other boys’ or the public’s phone usage—in particular, their ability to take and circulate photos of George. Even if George is a great kid, and by all accounts he is, neither his parents nor the school can stop onlookers taking photos or videos of him in the street.
“The couple’s biggest worry now is not the paparazzi, but an entire generation armed with camera phones, instantly uploading snaps and videos for ‘clout and likes,’ ” English writes in the Daily Mail.
It could be $100,000 or more. Although the days of newspapers and magazines paying huge amounts for scandalous images is over, if someone did snap a compromising photo of George, they could expect to get a large payday through syndication online and in print.
California paparazzo Mark Karloff says on his Paparazzi Podcast that in the past, he’d regularly make “$50,000 to $100,000 off one photo,” but now, if something sold for $1,000 in the paparazzi heyday, he says it would fetch more like $50 today.
A snapshot is one thing, but today we have video fears too. A candid video of teenage Prince George would get big numbers on social media, earning ad revenue with every click. So, it’s all added stress for George and his parents. “It will be interesting to see how they navigate this challenge given how determined they have always been to ring-fence their family from the moment George and his siblings were born,” writes English.
Kate is particularly worried about keeping her kids out of the spotlight because she’s experienced paparazzi intrusion both as a young woman and a mother.
Back in 2015, when George was a toddler, Kate was on a beach in Norfolk when she noticed they were being followed by two photographers. “She had to grab him and go, and was deeply upset about the whole thing,” English writes in the Daily Mail. “It wasn’t the first time this had happened, but she was really unhappy and very, very worried.”
Other candid photos of the young royals include:
Yes, there’s an ongoing agreement with the palace and the British press, meaning George and his siblings will be left alone at school, and private photos will not be published. This rule goes all the way back to when William and Harry were young.
It’s also certain that parents of children at Eton will be told not to publish images of the prince—a great rule for all parents to follow regarding children and their classmates, but even more pertinent in this case.
The wild card is, of course, the general public and social media. If anyone gets footage of George around town, it will be difficult to keep them from posting.

Every parent wants to believe they’ve done a good job and shaped their children to be polite, confident and well-balanced, but most of our little princes and princesses don’t regularly meet world leaders!

What is William and Kate’s biggest fear when it comes to Prince George?

It’s smartphones. William and Kate have been vocal about not letting their children have mobile phones, but once George follows in his father’s footsteps to the prestigious Eton boarding school in Berkshire, west of London, they may have to grapple with some modern realities.

Does George have a phone?

“I think children can access too much stuff they don’t need to see online,” William told Huck. “And so having a phone and text message, the old sort of ‘brick phone’ as they call them, I think that’s fine.”

Even if George is a great kid, and by all accounts he is, neither his parents nor the school can stop onlookers taking photos or videos of him in the street.

“The couple’s biggest worry now is not the paparazzi, but an entire generation armed with camera phones, instantly uploading snaps and videos for ‘clout and likes,’ ” English writes in the Daily Mail.

How much might a scandalous picture of George go for?

It could be $100,000 or more. Although the days of newspapers and magazines paying huge amounts for scandalous images is over, if someone did snap a compromising photo of George, they could expect to get a large payday through syndication online and in print.

California paparazzo Mark Karloff says on his Paparazzi Podcast that in the past, he’d regularly make “$50,000 to $100,000 off one photo,” but now, if something sold for $1,000 in the paparazzi heyday, he says it would fetch more like $50 today.

A snapshot is one thing, but today we have video fears too. A candid video of teenage Prince George would get big numbers on social media, earning ad revenue with every click. So, it’s all added stress for George and his parents. “It will be interesting to see how they navigate this challenge given how determined they have always been to ring-fence their family from the moment George and his siblings were born,” writes English.

What royal moments were caught on camera when William, Kate and the other royals were young?

Kate is particularly worried about keeping her kids out of the spotlight because she’s experienced paparazzi intrusion both as a young woman and a mother.

Back in 2015, when George was a toddler, Kate was on a beach in Norfolk when she noticed they were being followed by two photographers. “She had to grab him and go, and was deeply upset about the whole thing,” English writes in the Daily Mail. “It wasn’t the first time this had happened, but she was really unhappy and very, very worried.”

Other candid photos of the young royals include:

  • William at Eton: A smiling 13-year-old William was snapped walking down the street with his fellow pupils on his first day at Eton in 1995. After the death of Diana two years later, the British press stayed away from unauthorized images of the schoolboy.
  • Kate’s see-through dress: As a student at St. Andrews University in 2002, Catherine modeled a sheer dress and underwear on the catwalk at a university fashion show. Though not a paparazzi shot, the dress—and the runway photo—went down in history.
  • Harry’s Nazi costume: In 2005, Prince Harry attended a friend’s fancy-dress party in a Nazi uniform. A partygoer sold a photo of him to the Sun newspaper, which ran it with the headline, “Harry the Nazi.” He was forced to apologize at the time, but in his 2023 memoir, Spare, Harry blamed it on William and Catherine, who, he says, encouraged him to wear it.
  • Kate’s topless photos: In 2012, the newlyweds were on holiday in Provence, France, in a private property, when a paparazzi snapped topless photos of Catherine sunbathing. The images appeared in French Closer and Italian Chi magazines. The couple sued and French authorities ruled it an invasion of privacy.
  • Harry’s naked party pics: Also in 2012, Harry, still in his wild period, played strip pool with friends and others in a Las Vegas hotel suite. One of the women in attendance took a photo on her phone, which was obtained by TMZ. Harry again apologized but blamed it on the women. “I had counted on those dodgy girls showing some basic decency, and now I was going to pay the price forever,” he wrote in Spare. “These photos would never go away.”

Will the palace have a deal with the media to keep George’s life as private as possible?

Yes, there’s an ongoing agreement with the palace and the British press, meaning George and his siblings will be left alone at school, and private photos will not be published. This rule goes all the way back to when William and Harry were young.

It’s also certain that parents of children at Eton will be told not to publish images of the prince—a great rule for all parents to follow regarding children and their classmates, but even more pertinent in this case.

The wild card is, of course, the general public and social media. If anyone gets footage of George around town, it will be difficult to keep them from posting.
